<reason>A genuinely close, high-quality exchange. CON built a sharp dilemma (a bare sentence is either useless or demands individualized disclosure nobody would defend) and pressed it with memorable lines ("verdict with a middleman," "liturgy," "identical labels"). But CON's own concessions did damage: [A2.6] admitted the optimizer's edge "was never knowing ranking exists," which undercut the gaming harm, and [A2.7] endorsed regulator-facing disclosure and audits, which handed PRO the trilemma that framed the back half. PRO exploited both cleanly, defended the value of the notice as "the end of a false certainty" (prediction from photos ≠ verdict from two hundred humans — never squarely answered), and used the credit-score analogy to separate meaning from exploitability. CON's "three hands, three powers" answer is logically coherent, but it leaves CON defending the counterintuitive position that the ranked person is the one party who shouldn't be told, and CON's closing "any app can already say we don't rank" ignored PRO's credibility point from [B4.3]. PRO slightly overstated CON's concession as "zero gaming," a small cost, but overall PRO made the decisive clash clearer and easier to resolve for the motion as written.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's second rebuttal turning CON's own concessions into the regulator-versus-user contrast ([B4.5]-[B4.7]): "the ranking is important enough to tell a regulator, but not the person being ranked." CON's three-audiences reply was clever but could not dissolve the intuitive force of that framing.</best_rebuttal>
